material: Carbon fiber / resin over insulating foam
finding: The team selected a catamaran after modeling and a small model test. Drivetrain forces later damaged a motor: a fast hull still needs a compatible, supported shaft system.

route: Reuse 2025 hull; tune stern, steering and propulsion
finding: Stern foam experiments did not deliver the main breakthrough; propeller changes did. A rudder helped maintain stability on plane. Preserve time to tune the integrated boat.

route: Carved foam → fiberglass mold → carbon layup
finding: Steps were intended to reduce water contact at speed. Mold release failed and required repairs; CFD omitted waves and dynamic hull rise. Tooling and physical testing matter.

material: Inherited shell; glassed-in wood supports, aluminum rails
route: Reuse hull; build adjustable payload supports
finding: Strakes improved stability in simulation. Angled and asymmetric interior sides required tailored supports. Check usable mounting space, not just outside dimensions.

material: Inherited hull; wood supports, aluminum rails and printed trays
route: Reuse 2025 hull; revise battery and payload restraints
finding: The tapered bay made battery rails diverge, requiring a revised mounting arrangement. Strake benefits came from simulation; leave room for practical mounts and restraints.

route: CLC Cocktail Class Racer kit; stitch-and-glue assembly
finding: Selection balanced planing area, freeboard and kit availability. The team glassed the exterior and sealed bare wood. A conventional kit was compatible with a leading overall result.

material: Commercial hull; shell material not established here
route: Buy larger hull after testing a smaller donor
finding: The 65-inch donor sat too low during load testing. The larger deep-V was selected to improve freeboard and wake handling after prior-year ingress and steering problems.

material: Purchased kayak; shell resin not established here
route: Custom design abandoned when tooling suppliers could not meet schedule
finding: The intended custom hull could not be manufactured in time. The team switched to a kayak. Confirm tooling capacity and delivery before committing to a custom shell.

material: Fiberglass center hull, foam floats, PVC frame
route: Buy RC hull; add shaped foam outriggers
finding: The donor alone failed the team’s capacity test. Added floats supplied buoyancy and roll stability. Test the fully equipped hull before finalizing frame and deck geometry.

route: Acquire used jet ski through a repair exchange; refurbish
finding: High component placement caused more roll than expected. Outriggers improved stability but added drag and slightly reduced top speed. Beam alone cannot compensate for poor equipment placement.

material: Thermoformed marine MMA plastic + aluminum frame
route: Sponsored CNC wood mold → industrial thermoforming → team assembly
level: Documented design + manufacturing; race foiling unconfirmed
finding: The custom foil system needed an internal frame to carry foil and steering loads. More than 300 CAD hours preceded production. Plan the structure and supply chain with the foil geometry.

material: 2007 TIGA HyperX donor board; custom foils
route: Buy used board instead of fabricating a hull
finding: The flat-bottom board offered a ready-made planing platform so effort could focus on foils and propulsion. The paper’s takeoff and stability analysis is not proof of race foiling.
